collection_summary: Adapted / narrowed from seed #20 in datasets/pkdb_bench/docs/example_questions.txt ('For each decade of the 20th century, list 5 defining technological inventions with their inventor and country of origin.'). Cycle-0 staging applied the lessons learned from cycles 1-2 of world_religions_top5_holy_sites: (a) selection-framing rather than ranked-framing; (b) composite PK = (Decade, Milestone) with List Position as non-key numeric display ordinal. Cycle-1 audit (this instance) reframed 'technological inventions' to 'technological or scientific milestones' because several staged rows are discoveries (Nuclear fission 1939, DNA double-helix 1953) or large-scale projects (Manhattan Project Trinity test, Skylab, Voyager Program) rather than strict inventions; the cited per-decade Wikipedia articles include all three categories in their decade-defining technology narratives, so the broader 'milestones' framing is honestly source-defined. Tier B (manual_wikipedia) extraction. Universe is the 10 decades of the 20th century (1900s-1990s). Per-decade selections are drawn from each decade's Wikipedia overview article, supplemented by per-event/per-organization Wikipedia articles for rows where the per-decade article does not name the principal individual or organization (cycle-3 audit added Apple Inc. as the country anchor for the Macintosh row, bringing the total to 32 source URLs). Result: 10 decades x 5 milestones = 50 rows x 5 columns, composite PK on (Decade, Milestone), 0 duplicate PKs. Country column ranges over 8 distinct countries (USA dominant, plus UK, Germany, Italy, Poland, Switzerland, Soviet Union, Japan). Multi-attribute (Attributed To, Country) over the per-decade partition exercises the calibration goal of scaled_enumeration: well-known attributions (Wright Brothers, Marconi, Salk, Maiman, Berners-Lee) are very strong recall signals, while organizational attributions (NASA, IBM, Sony, DARPA, Manhattan Project, OKB-1) and lesser-known individual attributions (Czochralski, Schick, Watson-Watt, Atalla & Kahng) progressively exercise the confidence gradient.
source_coverage_notes:
Thirty-two Wikipedia source URLs combine to support the universe + per-decade selection + per-row attribution values (cycle-3 audit fix; was 31 after cycle-2, 27 after cycle-1, 12 at cycle-0 staging). Ten per-decade Wikipedia articles (1900s through 1990s) provide the universe + per-decade selection source. Twenty-two per-event/per-organization Wikipedia articles provide the article-supported attribution (named-individual or organization plus country) values for rows where the per-decade article does not name the principal attribution. The cycle-1 audit found that the cycle-0 source set was thin: many attribution/country values came from common knowledge rather than from the per-decade article's text; cycle-1 explicitly cites a per-row Wikipedia article wherever the per-decade article does not support the attribution/country value. Cycle-3 added Apple Inc. to support Country=USA on the Macintosh row (the Mac (computer) article supports Apple/Macintosh attribution but not the country explicitly). Note: Wikipedia 'Timeline of historic inventions' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_historic_inventions) was consulted at cycle-0 but not adopted as a source — its 20th-century section was not retrievable in a single fetch and the per-decade decade articles plus per-event articles already cover the staged rows; documenting the consulted-not-used status here so future curators do not re-explore the same path.

Identifies Teller as 'father of the hydrogen bomb' and documents the Teller-Ulam joint-attribution dispute; Stanislaw Ulam contributed the 1950 calculations and the 1951 design — the staged Attributed To cell preserves this dual attribution as 'Edward Teller & Stanislaw Ulam (Teller-Ulam design)'.

Article describes Kihara as 'best known for his work on the original Walkman cassette-tape player in the 1970s' — the staged Attributed To cell uses 'Sony (Nobutoshi Kihara)' to combine the organizational attribution from the Walkman article with the engineering credit from the Kihara article.

Country: USA (Boca Raton, Florida).

Verbatim: 'the original Macintosh was launched in January 1984 at US$2,495'; 'Conceived in 1979 by Jef Raskin, Macintosh was envisioned as an affordable, easy-to-use computer for the masses'; Steve Jobs took control of the project in 1981. Country: USA (Apple, Cupertino).
- source_urls[30] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_Hadron_Collider): value (1990s row 5). Cycle-2 audit fix: cited to support the LHC attribution to CERN and the Switzerland location. Verbatim: 'It was built by the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) between 1998 and 2008'; 'It lies in a tunnel 27 kilometres (17 mi) in circumference... beneath the France-Switzerland border near Geneva'. Country: Switzerland (with the tunnel straddling the Switzerland-France border).
- source_urls[31] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.): value (1980s row 2 — Country anchor). Cycle-3 audit fix: cited to support Country=USA for the Macintosh row. Verbatim: 'Apple Inc. is an American multinational technology company headquartered in Cupertino, California, in Silicon Valley'. The Mac (computer) article (source_urls[29]) supports the Apple-Macintosh attribution but does not explicitly state the country; this Apple Inc. article provides the country anchor.

Validation note: each row's Attributed To / Country value is now traceable to a specific Wikipedia article quote — either the per-decade article's text where it names the attribution, or the per-event article's text where the per-decade article is silent. The cycle-1 audit explicitly required this per-row citability and the source set is now expanded to support it.

Universe-size sanity: 10 decades of the 20th century is a fixed universe; 5 milestones per decade is the seed-stipulated partition shape; total 50 rows. Country distribution (8 distinct values) reflects the 20th-century science-and-technology development landscape: USA dominant (especially 1940s-1980s), UK strong (1910s-1930s, 1950s, 1980s-1990s), Germany (1900s-1930s), Japan (1960s-1990s), one entry each for Italy, Poland, Soviet Union, Switzerland.
decision_log:
Candidate card (Stage 1 pre-gate, then Stage 2 scored axes per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: PASS with two documented risks. R1: '5 defining technological inventions' is curator selection across multiple decades, not source-defined ranking — applied the world_religions_top5_holy_sites cycle-1+2 lessons upfront by reframing 'defining' as 'major' (selection framing) and using PK = (Decade, Milestone) with List Position as non-key numeric. R2: attribution / country is sometimes contested for landmark milestones (e.g., transistor has 3 named inventors, ARPANET is organizational, Manhattan Project has many contributors); the staged values follow the cited per-decade Wikipedia article's attribution where given, otherwise default to the per-event article's named individual or the lead organization. 50 rows >> the 10-row floor; 5-column shape with 1 partition key + 1 list-position ordinal + 1 entity key + 2 non-key text attributes; strong confidence gradient; LLM-knowable for major milestones; low temporal sensitivity (20th century is closed history).
- Seed/provenance: ADAPTED / NARROWED from seed #20 in example_questions.txt (line 34). The seed says 'list 5 defining technological inventions'; the staged title says 'list five major technological or scientific milestones' (cycle-1 broadened framing) to honestly reflect that the cited per-decade Wikipedia articles enumerate selections rather than ranked top-5 lists and include discoveries and large-scale projects alongside strict inventions.
- Category: scaled_enumeration — primary because the instance is a per-partition selection (5 milestones per decade) over a partitioned universe (10 decades) with multiple non-key attributes. The (Decade, Milestone) PK and union+filter operation_type follow the precedent of the films and world-religions scaled_enumeration instances.
- Source plan: 32 Wikipedia URLs (cycle-3) across 10 per-decade articles (universe + value) and 22 per-event/per-organization articles for rows where the per-decade article does not name the attribution or country. Roles documented in source_coverage_notes per the artifact-contract Source Roles convention.
- Expected shape: 10 x 5 = 50 rows x 5 cols, composite PK (Decade, Milestone). Realized: 50 x 5, 0 duplicates.
- Domain: Technology/Inventions — NEW family per domain_taxonomy.md (Technology was unrepresented before this instance).
- Risks/adaptation: per the two pre-gate risks above. Additional minor risk: some milestones are discoveries (Nuclear fission 1939, DNA double-helix 1953) or large-scale projects (Trinity test, Skylab, Voyager Program) rather than strict inventions; cycle-1 audit broadened the framing from 'inventions' to 'milestones' to honestly include these. The cited Wikipedia decade articles include all three categories in their technology-of-the-decade narratives, so they are honestly source-included. Selection-not-ranked framing is honest about not adjudicating whether each pick is the absolute 5th-most-important.
- Decision: STAGE.

Further decisions:
1) Per-decade selections were drawn from the Wikipedia decade overview article's most-emphasized technology entries. Where the article was thin (1960s emphasizes atomic-bomb proliferation; 1970s emphasizes NASA programs), supplemented with the most universally-recognized 1960s/1970s technology milestones and corroborated via per-event articles (Laser, LED, Computer mouse, ARPANET, Altair 8800, Walkman). The 1960s picks (Laser, LED, Bullet Train, Computer mouse, ARPANET) are universally cited as defining 1960s technologies; the 1970s picks (Intel 4004, Skylab, Altair 8800, Voyager, Walkman) balance Intel/personal-computing with NASA and consumer electronics.
2) Schema: composite PK is (Decade, Milestone) with List Position typed 'numeric' (non-key). This applies the cycle-2 lesson from world_religions_top5_holy_sites — for selected-not-ranked partitioned tables, the entity column should be the load-bearing key rather than the list-position ordinal. Milestone names are unique within and across decades in this dataset (verified at preflight), so (Decade, Milestone) gives a clean composite PK.
3) List Position values (1-5 per decade) record the curator's documented display order for each decade (per-decade rationale in decision_log; not a uniform source-defined ranking). Within each decade I tend to list earlier-year milestones first (chronological within decade), with ties broken by the cited article's order of mention.
4) Attributed To column (renamed from 'Inventor' at cycle-2 audit; cycle-1 broadened the column semantic from 'inventor' to 'attributed individual or organization'; cycle-2 renamed for accuracy): where the cited Wikipedia article names individuals, those are used (Wright Brothers, Theodore Maiman, Tim Berners-Lee). Where the article credits an organization or company, that is used (NASA, IBM, Sony, Warner Brothers, DARPA, Manhattan Project, OKB-1, CERN). Multi-individual joint attributions use ' & ' as the separator (e.g., 'John Bardeen & Walter Brattain & William Shockley' for the transistor) following the Wikipedia article's joint attribution.
5) Country column: 'country of origin' is interpreted as the country most associated with the milestone's development — typically the attributed-person's nationality (Wright Brothers -> USA) or the country of the company / lab where the milestone occurred (Bell Labs USA for transistor and MOSFET; CERN Switzerland for LHC). For Marconi (Italian inventor working in UK at the time of his 1901 transatlantic transmission), the cited 1900s Wikipedia article gives 'Italy/UK'; the staged value uses 'Italy' as the attributed-person's country of origin to match the seed's 'country of origin' phrasing. Document the choice.
6) Decade format uses the lowercase plural form '1900s', '1910s', '1990s' rather than '1900-1909' or '1900–1909' to match Wikipedia article titles ('1900s_(decade)', '1910s', '1990s').
7) The 'Soviet Union' label (Sputnik 1957) is used because the Soviet Union was the political-state attribution at the time of the milestone, even though the country no longer exists. This matches Wikipedia's convention for historical attributions.
normalization_decisions: Decade values use the lowercase plural form '1900s' through '1990s', matching Wikipedia article title conventions. 'Milestone' column (cycle-2 rename from 'Invention') uses the Wikipedia article title or the article's primary phrasing (e.g., 'ENIAC general-purpose electronic computer', 'Intel 4004 microprocessor', 'Sputnik 1 (first artificial satellite)') and may name inventions, discoveries, or large-scale projects depending on the cited per-decade article's framing. 'Attributed To' column (cycle-2 rename from 'Inventor', cycle-1 broadened from invented-by-only to attributed-individual-or-organization): individuals listed by full name where the article gives one (Wright Brothers, Tim Berners-Lee); organizations listed by their commonly cited form (NASA, IBM, Sony, Warner Brothers, Apple, Nintendo, CERN, DARPA, Manhattan Project, OKB-1, Eastman Kodak, Japanese National Railways); multi-individual joint attributions use ' & ' as the separator (e.g., 'John Bardeen & Walter Brattain & William Shockley'); combined organization+individual attributions use parentheses (e.g., 'Sony (Nobutoshi Kihara)', 'Sony (using Akira Yoshino's design)'). Country values use standard short-form names (USA, UK, Germany, Italy, Poland, Switzerland, Japan) plus 'Soviet Union' for historical attributions where the political state at the time matches the milestone. Country column reflects 'country of origin' as the country most associated with the milestone's development (typically the attributed-person's nationality or the lab/company's country); for Marconi's 1901 transatlantic radio (Italian inventor working in UK), the staged value is 'Italy' to match the seed's 'country of origin' phrasing — document the alternative 'Italy/UK' framing in decision_log. List Position is a 1-5 within-decade ordinal recording the curator's documented display order (per-decade rationale: typically chronological within decade with ties broken by the cited article's order of mention). Sort order is (Decade ASC, List Position ASC).
open_questions: 1) The Technology family target is 5 instances per instance_selection_priorities.md; this is the first. Future Technology instances could include 'major operating systems x first-release year x developer', 'top programming languages by current usage', or 'milestones in space exploration'. 2) Cycle-1 audit broadened the framing from 'inventions' to 'milestones' to honestly include discoveries (Nuclear fission, DNA double-helix) and large-scale projects (Manhattan Project Trinity test, Skylab, Voyager Program) alongside strict inventions; a future audit could re-narrow to 'strict inventions only' which would require replacing 5-7 rows. 3) The 1960s decade Wikipedia article is thin on technology specifics; the staged 1960s entries are anchored to per-invention articles (Laser, LED, Tōkaidō Shinkansen, Computer mouse, ARPANET) which are now first-class source_urls entries. 4) Marconi's 1901 transatlantic radio is staged with country='Italy' (inventor's nationality) but the cited 1900s article also offers 'Italy/UK' (work location). The audit may prefer either. 5) Apollo Moon Landing (1969) is not staged for the 1960s even after the cycle-1 'milestones' reframe; the staged 1960s rows already cover Laser, LED, Bullet train, Computer mouse, and ARPANET — adding Apollo would require dropping one of those. A future curator could substitute Apollo Moon Landing in for ARPANET if the partition emphasis shifts toward space technology. 6) The Walkman attribution was changed at cycle-1 from 'Sony (Masaru Ibuka)' to 'Sony (Nobutoshi Kihara)' because the Walkman article credits Ibuka with conceiving the idea but the Kihara article is the only Wikipedia article that explicitly names a Walkman engineer; the audit recommended this fix. A future curator could refine to 'Sony (Norio Ohga, designer)' if a stronger source supports Ohga's design role. 7) The Sputnik 1 attribution was changed at cycle-1 from 'Sergei Korolev' to 'OKB-1 (Mikhail S. Khomyakov)' per the Sputnik 1 article's explicit chief-constructor citation; a future curator could refine to 'Sergei Korolev (project leader)' if the source emphasis warrants. 8) The Hydrogen bomb attribution was changed at cycle-1 from 'Edward Teller' to 'Edward Teller & Stanislaw Ulam (Teller-Ulam design)' to honestly reflect the disputed co-attribution; the Edward Teller article documents the dispute. 9) The 'Significance Note' column from world_religions_top5_holy_sites is not present here because the seed-stipulated schema is (Invention, Inventor, Country) — only 2 non-key text attributes vs world religions' 3 (City, Country, Significance Note). The cycle-2 audit renamed Invention -> Milestone and Inventor -> Attributed To to honestly reflect the broadened semantics, but the column count and seed-schema continuity are preserved.

blocking_addressed: Scope-related: cycle-0 staged title 'list five major technological inventions' was strict-invention-framed, but several staged rows are discoveries (Nuclear fission 1939, DNA double-helix 1953) or large-scale projects (Atomic bomb / Manhattan Project Trinity test, Skylab Space Station, Voyager Program) rather than single-event inventions. Cycle-1 fix: broadened table_title and db_analog framing from 'inventions' to 'technological or scientific milestones' which the cited per-decade Wikipedia articles all support (each decade article includes discoveries and projects in its decade-defining technology narrative). Column name 'Inventor' is retained for seed-schema continuity but the column semantic is broadened to 'attributed individual or organization' and is documented in normalization_decisions. No CSV row removals; the broader framing is honestly source-supported.

Structural: cycle-0 staged source_urls had 12 entries (10 per-decade articles + 2 per-invention articles for Laser and Computer mouse) but many inventor/country values came from common knowledge rather than from the per-decade article's text. Cycle-1 fix: source_urls expanded from 12 to 27 with 15 per-invention/per-event Wikipedia articles added for rows where the per-decade article does not name the principal individual or organization: ENIAC, Transistor, Microwave oven, Edward Teller, Sputnik 1, Light-emitting diode, ARPANET, Tōkaidō Shinkansen, Intel 4004, Altair 8800, Walkman, Nobutoshi Kihara, Lithium-ion battery, Gene therapy, Dolly (sheep). source_count updated from 12 to 27. Source Roles block in source_coverage_notes documents each URL's role with verbatim quotes from the cited article supporting the staged inventor/country value.

Factual: cycle-0 staged Walkman inventor was 'Sony (Masaru Ibuka)', but the Walkman Wikipedia article does NOT name Ibuka as inventor — it credits Ibuka with conceiving the idea, Norio Ohga with the design request, and Akio Morita with leadership. The auditor flagged this as not source-supported. Cycle-1 fix: changed inventor to 'Sony (Nobutoshi Kihara)' because the Nobutoshi Kihara Wikipedia article explicitly states he is 'best known for his work on the original Walkman cassette-tape player in the 1970s' — this is the strongest article-supported individual attribution. Both Walkman and Nobutoshi Kihara articles added to source_urls. Three additional inventor cells were also corrected at cycle-1 to align with article-supported attribution: (a) Sputnik 1 from 'Sergei Korolev' to 'OKB-1 (Mikhail S. Khomyakov)' per the Sputnik 1 article's chief-constructor citation; (b) Hydrogen bomb from 'Edward Teller' to 'Edward Teller & Stanislaw Ulam (Teller-Ulam design)' per the Edward Teller article's documented co-inventor dispute with Ulam; (c) Lithium-ion battery from 'Sony' to 'Sony (using Akira Yoshino's design)' per the Lithium-ion battery article's verbatim 'using Yoshino's design' phrasing; (d) ARPANET from 'DARPA (Bob Taylor)' to 'DARPA' because Bob Taylor 'initiated the project in 1966' rather than inventing it; (e) Dolly the sheep from 'Ian Wilmut' to 'Ian Wilmut (Roslin Institute)' to add the institutional anchor. Five inventor-cell corrections in total.

Structural: schema rename — cycle-1 broadened the column semantic from 'inventions' to 'milestones' (table_title, framing) but left the column names 'Invention' and 'Inventor' unchanged, which the cycle-2 audit flagged as inconsistent. Updated CSV header, draft.json::columns, draft.json::primary_key (Decade, Invention) -> (Decade, Milestone), draft.json::column_types, draft.json::db_analog (referenced milestone and attributed_to), and the corresponding narratives in collection_summary, source_coverage_notes, decision_log, normalization_decisions, _extraction_notes, and temporal_note. CSV row data values unchanged (50 rows, same content); only the column headers and meta-field names changed.

Structural: missing value-role sources — cycle-1 added 15 per-event articles to source_urls but the cycle-2 audit identified 4 rows whose attribution/country was still not supported by the cited per-decade article alone: DNA double-helix (1950s row 2; needed Watson-Crick paper article), IBM PC (1980s row 1; needed IBM Personal Computer article), Macintosh (1980s row 2; needed Mac (computer) article), and LHC (1990s row 5; needed Large Hadron Collider article). Cycle-2 fix: added these 4 articles to source_urls. source_count moved from 27 to 31. Each new URL has a documented Roles: block entry with verbatim quotes supporting the staged attribution and country values: Watson-Crick paper anchors DNA at Cambridge UK; IBM Personal Computer anchors IBM/Boca Raton USA; Mac (computer) anchors Apple/Cupertino USA; LHC anchors CERN/Switzerland-France border.
hygiene_addressed: Scrubbed stale cycle-0 narrative wording: source_coverage_notes opening line updated from 'Twenty-seven Wikipedia source URLs ... was 12 in cycle 0' to 'Thirty-one Wikipedia source URLs ... was 27 after cycle-1, was 12 at cycle-0 staging' to capture the full source-count history. suggestion_addressed: Suggestion (per the cycle-1 re-audit): consider whether 'Attributed To' or 'Originator' is the cleanest column name. Adopted 'Attributed To' rather than 'Originator' because (a) the column already encompasses individuals, organizations, and joint attributions where 'Originator' would feel imprecise for organizational entries (NASA, IBM, OKB-1), and (b) 'Attributed To' is closer to the seed's 'inventor and country of origin' phrasing while honestly broadening to non-strict-inventor attributions. Decision recorded so future curators do not re-litigate.
